 Why Korea? BTS, skincare and K-drama, tourists say 
 Published : Nov. 18, 2026 - 15:25:52
 Hong Yoo 
 Add The Korea Herald on Google
 Link copied!
 Korea celebrated a record 20 million foreign visitors this week; travelers at Incheon Airport share what drew them to the country
 Foreign tourists pose for photos at Gyeongbokgung in Jongno-gu, Seoul, on Nov. 12, the day the Culture Ministry announced that foreign arrivals to Korea had surpassed 20 million in a single year for the first time. (Yonhap) Nicole Alcaino and Camila Galaz encountered a problem many travelers leaving Korea do: On the last day of their three-week vacation, the two friends from Chile stood by their open suitcases at Incheon Airport, rearranging souvenirs to get under the airline’s weight limit.
 “We spent all of the days in Olive Young. All this is skincare. Serums, toners, lip glosses, everything. We learned about them on TikTok,” Galaz said.
 That was Tuesday, the same day Korea held a ceremony at the airport to mark, for the first time, more than 20 million foreign visitors in a single year. The Korea Herald asked travelers passing through the airport why they chose Korea.
 Skincare came up most, followed by BTS and K-dramas. Many also named things harder to put in a tourism ad, like clean streets, safe nights and nice people.
 Nicole Alcaino (left) and Camila Galaz (right), tourists from Chile, share about their trip to Korea at Incheon Airport’s Terminal 2 on Nov. 17. (Hong Yoo/The Korea Herald) It was the first trip to Korea for Galaz and Alcaino. Galaz has a friend who visits every year, and that friend's recommendation brought them here. They came looking forward to "basically everything," Galaz said, from skincare and K-pop to K-dramas and food. They visited N Seoul Tower and Seoul Forest, and spent three days in Busan.
 For Latin Americans, she said, the draw is price.
 “Skincare is so expensive there, and here it’s so, so, so cheap,” she said.
 Fabiola, from Mexico, was on her first visit to Korea with Jorge, who was on his third. Her plan was simple.
 “I want to buy skincare. I’ve heard about Olive Young,” she said.
 For Ariba Noman, a Canadian exchange student at Korea University, K-beauty was also the first connection to Korean culture, ahead of K-pop and K-dramas. Since moving to Seoul in August, she has gotten into Korean food and local fashion brands.
 Tommy (left) and his wife, Renee, from Portland, Oregon, pose at Incheon Airport’s Terminal 2 on Nov. 17 at the end of a three-week trip across Korea. (Hong Yoo/The Korea Herald) Following BTS 
 Joy Reyes, an American who has visited Korea more than 10 times, has followed BTS since their debut. She and her husband run a business in the US, and she has long pointed to the seven-member group as a model of teamwork.
 “If seven people stick together, they can accomplish anything. So, seeing where they're at today is amazing. We really want to go to their concert someday. We weren't able to get tickets to the March 21 concert,” she said.
 For Tommy and Renee, a married couple from Portland, Oregon, K-dramas came first. Over three weeks in Korea, they wore hanbok at Gyeongbokgung, watched BTS in a movie theater and traveled to Nami Island, Sokcho in Gangwon Province, and Jeju Island. They ended in Pohang, North Gyeongsang Province, where “Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha” was filmed.
 “That was the K-drama that got us into Korea in the first place, so it was only right that we finished our stay in Pohang,” said Tommy.
 He said the shows have "wholesome, good, moral values," and Renee added that they showed her a culture of respecting elders.
 Some of their favorite moments had nothing to do with TV, like riding the bus and laughing with ajummas, and eating raw abalone with soju from haenyeo, Jeju’s women divers. At a small restaurant in a village outside Seogwipo, they were the only Americans.
 “The food and the experience were wonderful,” said Renee.
 Joy Reyes (left), her daughter Claire and Daniel Reyes from the US, pose at Incheon Airport’s Terminal 2 on Nov. 17. The family has visited Korea more than 10 times since 2023. (Hong Yoo/The Korea Herald) Safe, clean and easy to get around 
 The Reyes family first came on a cruise stop in January 2023 and has returned every year since. Earlier this year, Joy Reyes and her daughter, Claire, took Hangul classes at Korea University. Asked what keeps drawing the family back, her husband, Daniel Reyes, didn’t hesitate.
 “It’s safe. It’s clean. I can’t say enough about how clean the country is everywhere,” he said.
 Joy Reyes also gets treatment for back pain at Gangnam Severance Hospital.
 “I can come here to get my treatment in one day, what takes me six weeks to get done in the US. So healthcare, phenomenal,” she said.
 Ariba Noman from Canada holds a bottle of banana milk she bought at a convenience store right after landing at Incheon Airport’s Terminal 2 on Nov. 17. (Hong Yoo/The Korea Herald) Noman and her classmate Dalal Abdurazag were returning from a short trip to Japan, and both said they missed Korea while they were gone. After landing, Noman went straight to an airport convenience store for a bottle of banana milk, and Abdurazag picked up a samgak gimbap, a triangle-shaped rice ball.
 “It’s a city that really, really cares about its people. And you can see it in the small details, like the heated seats at the bus stops,” said Noman.
 “Being women, sometimes you’re a little bit worried to go out. But we found that here it’s so safe. Public transport, especially at night, is such a blessing to have,” said Abdurazag.
 At the ceremony Tuesday, Culture Minister Chae Hwi-young said the ministry will prepare to host 30 million visitors a year, and eventually 40 million.
 Most travelers already had plans to come back. Galaz and Alcaino are thinking about December next year. Renee had a date in mind, too.
 "There's too much fun stuff to do. You can't do it in one trip, even if it's almost a month long. We're coming back in September," she said.
